prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, well-defined achievement: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while many atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group brought the scheme to the 1e-18 regime and added many-body clock physics. It is confirmed by independent clocks (Sr, Yb, Hg) and international comparisons, and it already feeds relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the discussion of redefining the second. The two-name structure is clean and the topic has not been recognised by earlier prizes on the frequency comb and ion clocks. After the opening round it is the only candidate that two members place first and six of eight members rank at all, which I read as breadth of support, but my own case rests on the physics, not the count.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is category: some colleagues will see this as a superb refinement of measurement rather than a discovery of new physics, and the allocation question is real because Lemonde, Pfau and others in the Sr/Yb community, and the Boulder group more broadly, contributed to the same development. Three members place it fourth or lower (Pearce fourth, Danielsson and Mehlig fifth) and Olsson third, so support is wide but not deep. Twisted bilayer graphene or Hubbard-model quantum simulation could be argued to offer a more novel scientific result.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clock first as an instrument-level breakthrough, with Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength concept as the decisive origin and Ye's group providing record accuracy and many-body clock work.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name attribution, and I would add that the concept alone is not the prize: it took the Boulder demonstrations of coherence and systematic control to turn it into a standard. I would resist framing it purely as 'what we can measure'. The many-body clock results and the use of the clock as a probe of interactions and relativity are physics results, and the citation should say so rather than lean only on metrology.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a theory-then-experiment discovery with a clear before and after, opening a tunable platform for correlated phases, while placing the clock third.
responses.response: I take the novelty argument seriously, and I ranked B029 second myself. My disagreement is about maturity: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and Olsson herself notes that eight years is short, while the clock has a decade-long record of independent confirmation. I would not call B029 premature, but I see it as the natural next candidate, not the one to prefer this year. If the committee is inclined to favour a condensed-matter discovery, I would want the credit to the earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto addressed explicitly.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first and the clock fifth, noting that the clock is mature, and that the argument for a conceptual advance in statistical physics is stronger than for a measurement tool.
responses.response: I accept that fluctuation theorems are a conceptual advance and that the experimental confirmations are real. But the four-name credit, with Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert, and the long Evans-Cohen-Morriss lineage make attribution much harder than for the clock, where two names map onto two clear contributions. A committee that cannot choose three names confidently in B032 should be cautious. I would also say the clock is not merely a tool: it has tightened bounds on variation of constants and enabled a new class of experiments.

responses.point: Pearce places the clock fourth, finding the science mature and the 1e-18 regime transformative, but he notes that the redefinition of the second has not happened and that other clock groups contributed.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition is still pending, but the prize should reward the demonstrated performance and independent agreement between clocks, not the formal decision of a metrology body that follows its own timetable. On contributors, I accept his list of Paris, Braunschweig and Boulder groups and I think the committee should consider whether a two-name prize is defensible, which I believe it is, given Katori's proposal and Ye's leading role in accuracy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a metrology instrument as a discovery within the intent of the physics prize.
How to weigh the contributions of the broader Sr/Yb clock community (Lemonde, Pfau and others) against the two credited names.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second would be read as a sign of immaturity or as evidence of impact.
My own judgement of the condensed-matter candidates, especially B029, rests on general standards rather than expertise.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile, I have a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, papers with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and training in Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group. None of these is a documented connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, so no specific conflict is apparent for B043. If the committee turned to a candidate involving close Lund or ETH colleagues I would disclose the connection and consider recusal. I am an atomic physicist and my views on B043, B006 and B027 may be tied to my field.
